extracted.intended_audience: employers, petitioners, immigration attorneys, policy analysts, and public commenters on the H-1B weighted-selection rule
extracted.subtask_description: Final-rule preamble responses to public comments on DHS's proposed weighted selection process for H-1B cap allocations, covering data and modeling choices, alternatives, costs, benefits, distributional effects, and administrative impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use petition data to estimate wage-level distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS uses petition data (not registration data) to estimate the wage-level distribution of the registration population because LCAs are not required for registrations and wage levels are verified at the petition stage via the associated LCA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merging registrations with LCA data would be noisy and potentially misleading because registrations currently do not include verified wage level information, not every registration can be cleanly merged with an LCA, and many registrations never mature into petitions. Using petition data ensures wage levels are validated and provides a reliable basis for analysis, though DHS acknowledges limitations in estimating registration-stage impacts from petition data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficiary-centric registration anchoring and lowest-wage assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor the registration process to real registration entries by applying a beneficiary-centric approach that reduces duplicate registrations and assigns the lowest wage level across multiple registrations for the same beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces incentives for gaming and creates a consistent beneficiary-level input for weighting. Because the lowest wage level will govern selection probability when multiple registrations are submitted for the same beneficiary or for multiple worksites, unique beneficiaries have less incentive to have multiple registrations at different wage levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooled (single-draw) modeling is acceptable when tractable
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling the weighted selection as a single pooled draw across all registrations is more tractable and clarifies the rule’s impact, even if advanced-degree and regular-cap registrant distributions differ slightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a two-step model (advanced degree pool then regular pool) is theoretically different, the difference is small because only 20,000 of 85,000 slots are in the advanced-degree exemption and the wage mixes are broadly similar. A pooled model entails minor loss of accuracy but improves tractability and clarity of impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and illustrations should state scope and avoid implying absence
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures that present only the top n occupations (e.g., top five six-digit SOC codes) should be titled and interpreted as illustrative of distributional changes and not as implying zero petitions in occupations or wage levels not shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing only the top five, clarify that absence from the figure does not mean zero petitions at that wage level; correct any misstatements in the NPRM that implied nonexistence of petitions for omitted codes. Such presentation choices do not affect underlying analysis if properly described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify distributional effects and transfers where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory impact analysis should quantify transfers and evaluate distributional effects across SOC codes and by firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS's RIA and IRFA present impacts by SOC codes and firm size; geography is normalized by prevailing wages by occupation and area to mitigate systematic advantage for higher-cost regions. Where commenters assert transfers (e.g., employers to workers), DHS should quantify transfers if data and methodology permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to monetize impacts lacking reliable data
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not isolate or monetize speculative macro impacts (e.g., offshoring decisions or declines in foreign student enrollment) without reliable public data or a credible methodology linking the rule causally to those outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asserting such impacts must provide data or a methodology. DHS declines to model offshoring or enrollment impacts when there is no reliable data on how many jobs are offshored due to unsuccessful H-1B petitions or how decisions would change because of this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reasonable alternatives but prioritize policy objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives (pure random selection, partial or steep weighting, geographic/occupation carve-outs, set-asides for small entities) should be considered, but DHS will select the approach that best achieves the policy objective of facilitating admission of higher-skilled, higher-paid beneficiaries while maintaining administrability and program integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining pure random selection (even with anti-fraud) does not advance the objective and leaves incentives for mass low-wage registration. Partial weighting produces modest changes; steep weighting risks functioning as a carve-out and crowding out lower wage levels. Geographic/occupation carve-outs increase complexity, subjectivity, and susceptibility to gaming. Preference schemes for small entities may undermine the rule's overall utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted selection must remain administrable, predictable, and transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighting ratios should be designed to be administrable, predictable, and transparent; extreme weighting that dramatically alters year-to-year variation is disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steep weighting could create disproportionate selection distributions, exclude lower wage levels, and exacerbate annual volatility. DHS declines aggressive weighting that would effectively exclude level I and II workers or make selection outcomes unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevailing wage normalization by occupation and area
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prevailing wages by occupation and area of intended employment to normalize for local labor markets when weighting selection probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach mitigates systematic advantage for higher-cost regions and reduces the need for explicit geographic carve-outs. Weighting is applied with reference to Office of Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) wage levels tied to occupation and area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-fraud measures are complementary, not substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-fraud tools should complement the allocation mechanism but cannot by themselves replace allocation changes intended to alter incentives (e.g., mass registration at low wage levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While anti-fraud measures are important, they do not eliminate the incentive structure that a weighted allocation addresses. DHS considers anti-fraud tools supportive of, but not alternatives to, weighted selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic impact estimates should be transparent about data and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sufficient detail in the rulemaking record for public evaluation of estimates (e.g., wage gain calculations) without necessarily releasing individual-level raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS converted pay frequencies to annual amounts using standard factors (hourly×2,080; weekly×52; monthly×12; annual as reported), computed means, and top-coded annualized wages at $1,000,000 to mitigate extreme outliers. DHS asserts these steps and accompanying tables provide adequate transparency for review even if raw microdata are withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-code extreme wage outliers to protect analysis integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigate undue influence from extreme high values and apparent entry errors by top-coding annualized wages (DHS used $1,000,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reviewed lower-tail data and found no anomalies, so no bottom-coding or exclusions were applied. Top-coding helps preserve distributional analysis without releasing raw data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative burden costing must be evidence-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of additional time and costs for registrants and petitioners should be based on documented time increases (e.g., 20 minutes for registrants, 15 minutes for petition form) and translated into annualized cost estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS estimates additional annual costs (approximately $15 million for registrants, $15 million for petitioners, $30 million total) and will require empirical support from commenters challenging those figures. Unsupported assertions of higher burden will be discounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not shift legal obligations on employer wages beyond existing law
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not create new employer wage liabilities; employers remain legally obligated to pay at least the prevailing wage or actual wage, whichever is higher (INA sec. 212(n)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not mandate employers to artificially raise wages; differentiated wages are already required under existing law as necessary to comply with prevailing wage obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted selection increases relative selection probabilities by wage level but cannot guarantee target distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighted selection process increases relative selection probabilities for higher wage levels but will not guarantee elimination or reduction to any specified target for level I or II selections if the registration pool is heavily concentrated at those levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If level I registrations massively outnumber higher-level registrations, level I will still receive a substantial share even after weighting. The rule is intended to shift odds and incentives, not to exclude participation by lower-wage filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence claiming macro harms must establish causality and provide data
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asserting that the rule will cause large macro harms (e.g., reduced innovation, offshoring, loss of foreign students) should provide empirical evidence, case-level data, or a credible causal methodology linking the rule to those outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS treats generalized macro literature on immigration benefits as background but will not attribute macro-level effects to this specific allocation mechanism without data demonstrating causal links. Absent such evidence, DHS considers such claims speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess impacts on USCIS operations and fees if rule increases costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate IT updates and additional adjudicator time; if the rule increases USCIS costs, fee schedule adjustments would be determined in the next comprehensive biennial fee review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges potential operational impacts and will address cost recovery through existing fee-review processes rather than in the rule itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present both program-wide and granular occupational wage distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide wage-distribution information at program-wide (two-digit SOC major group) and granular (six-digit SOC) levels to orient readers to both broad patterns and detailed occupation-level effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use program-wide figures for overview and six-digit SOC figures for granular analysis; clarify when figures are illustrative and limited to top occupations so they are not misinterpreted as exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between benefits vs transfers in RIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate estimates of increased wages paid (first‑year effect, e.g., $502 million) from transfer calculations (e.g., $858 million annual transfer) and explain whether figures represent new economic value or redistribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS's RIA reports both the increased total wages paid among selected cap-subject workers and separately reports the wage transfer effects that arise from reallocating selections from level I to higher wage levels within a fixed cap.
